notes.b: Pastries are grouped by how the fat is incorporated into the flour, and this decides their texture.
points: Short pastries (shortcrust, sweet shortcrust, suet and biscuit pastry): the fat is rubbed into the flour so that it coats the flour particles and limits gluten, giving a crumbly texture.
Puff pastries (rough puff, puff and flaky): pieces or layers of fat are folded into the dough, so layers of dough and fat separate and rise, giving a flaky texture.
Choux pastry: a cooked paste of water, fat and flour, with beaten egg added; it contains no rubbed-in fat and rises by steam into a hollow shell, as in eclairs and profiteroles.
Filo pastry: very thin sheets of dough layered with fat or oil, which become crisp when baked, as in spring rolls.
Suet pastry: made with shredded suet and self-raising flour, and steamed or boiled, as in a steamed pudding.

notes.b: Shortcrust is the most common short pastry and forms the base for sweet and savoury tarts and pies.
points: Ingredients: plain flour, a pinch of salt, cold fat (butter, margarine or lard) in roughly half the weight of the flour, and cold water to bind; sugar is added for sweet shortcrust.
Step 1: sift the flour and salt into a bowl, which aerates the flour and removes lumps.
Step 2: rub the cold fat into the flour with the fingertips until the mixture resembles fine breadcrumbs.
Step 3: add cold water gradually, mixing with a round-bladed knife until the dough just comes together.
Step 4: knead lightly, wrap and chill the dough so the gluten relaxes and the fat firms.
Step 5: roll lightly on a floured surface, line the tin, and chill again before baking.
Step 6: bake in a preheated hot oven until golden, then reduce the heat if the pastry is browning too quickly.
Presentation: sweet shortcrust is dusted with icing sugar or glazed; savoury shortcrust is used for quiche and pies, with the edges crimped.

notes.b: Rough puff is a puff pastry in which the fat is left in pieces rather than rubbed in, and it is folded in several turns to create layers.
points: Ingredients: plain flour, a pinch of salt, cold fat (butter or block margarine), and cold water to bind.
Step 1: cut the cold fat into irregular pieces, leave them visible and mix them lightly with the flour, binding the dough with cold water.
Step 2: roll the dough into a long rectangle, fold the bottom third up and the top third down, then turn the dough a quarter turn.
Step 3: repeat the roll, fold and turn several times, chilling between turns so the fat stays firm and the layers stay distinct.
Step 4: roll to the required thickness and chill before cutting so that the edges stay sharp.
Step 5: bake in a very hot preheated oven; the water in the fat turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, so the pastry rises and becomes flaky.
Presentation: sausage rolls, vol-au-vents and pie toppings; the layers should be even and golden, with sharp edges.
Keep the ingredients, hands, utensils and kitchen cool so that the fat does not melt before baking.
Weigh ingredients accurately so that the flour-to-fat ratio is correct.
Add cold liquid gradually; too much liquid makes the pastry tough and increases shrinkage.
Avoid overhandling: working the dough develops gluten, which makes pastry tough.
Rest and chill pastry before rolling and baking so that the gluten relaxes and the pastry does not shrink.
Roll evenly and lightly, and avoid stretching the dough, which causes shrinkage.
Bake in a preheated hot oven, and use blind baking for fillings that are not baked, such as quiche, which keeps the base crisp.

keyTerms.definition: A short pastry made by rubbing cold fat into flour and binding with cold water, giving a crumbly texture.
A puff pastry in which pieces of fat are folded into the dough in several turns to form flaky layers.

A pastry made from very thin sheets of dough layered with fat or oil, which become crisp when baked.
A pastry made with shredded suet and self-raising flour, which is steamed or boiled.
Working cold fat into flour with the fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs.

questions.prompt: Name three guidelines that help a student make a light shortcrust pastry, and explain why each one helps.
questions.model: Keep ingredients and utensils cool, so the fat does not melt and the pastry stays short. Handle the dough as little as possible, because overhandling develops gluten and makes the pastry tough. Add cold water gradually, so the dough is bound without becoming sticky or tough. Other acceptable guidelines include chilling before rolling, rolling lightly and using a preheated hot oven.

questions.prompt: Describe the preparation, cooking and presentation of rough puff pastry, and explain the principles a cook must follow for the pastry to rise evenly and become flaky.
questions.model: Preparation: cold fat is cut into pieces and mixed with flour and salt, then bound with cold water to form a dough. Folding: the dough is rolled into a rectangle, folded in three and turned a quarter turn, then this is repeated several times with chilling between turns, so that layers of dough and fat form. Cooking: the pastry is baked in a very hot preheated oven; the water in the fat turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, so the pastry rises and becomes flaky. Presentation: it is cut to size, with sharp edges, and used for sausage rolls, vol-au-vents or pie toppings, with even, golden layers. Principles: keep the fat cool so it stays in pieces; do not overhandle the dough; chill between turns and before cutting; roll evenly and avoid stretching; use a hot oven and do not let the fat melt before baking.
